speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I suggest that on
the question of reductions generally I agree with what has been said, that as the work of the Public Works Department is being restricted it certainly should not lead to an increased expenditure. But may I not submit that it is rather unreasonable to expect that a new minister who has only recently taken office would be able to reorganize his department in a few days and determine what reductions should be made? He is bound to take the estimates of last year as his basis. If later on. he can reduce the staff, well and good. Take the question of dismissals, the minister may find the number of his officials is greater than is needed, and if a proposal is made to dismiss those men summarily he will find very strong representations made as to the hardship entailed. I submit it is fair and reasonable for the House to expect reductions, but that it is not reasonable to expect them to be made right away. It seems to me that it is not unfair that ministers should ask for their estimates pretty much on the lines of last year, and the House should rely on them, with the money placed at their disposal, to make every reasonable effort during the year to guard against increased expenditure-I do not think the House expects the Minister of Public Works, or any other minister, with the short time at his disposal to be able to reorganize his department at the present time.

I do not think any
member of the House would say that we have been unmindful of the fact that the Minister of Public Works is new to his office. We have kept that in mind in all our questions and criticisms. We are simply seeking to get at the facts. The minister has made, not boasts, perhaps, but has taken credit for a reduction of thirty persons in the civil government vote. Now will he be good enough to tell us, as did the Postmaster General a few minutes ago, when these thirty reductions were made? I know there have been retirements from the Department of Public Works, especially large numbers of retirements from the engineer's branch.

Seven of the
reductions were due to death, seven to resignation, seven to retirement, and there were eleven transfers.

When were the seven
retired?

Five in July
1921; one in July 1922-

Hardly; we are not
there yet.
They are practically all in July 1921, except one.

All the retirements
were made in July 1921?
Yes.
Did not all the resignations also take place about the same time?
The resignations took place in May, July, October and December last year.

So the retirements and resignations all took place last year, and the rest are due to death, so the entire reduction in staff is due to Providence and the late government. Now we will see to whom the increase in staff is due. I remember quite well that in the engineering branch to which the minister has referred, page 42, very substantial reductions were made in the face of bitter criticism. I would just like to know whether it is to avoid some of those reductions that the thirteen men are brought from that branch now and added to the civil government vote under contingencies.
These thirteen were not concerned in that reduction.

These are thirteen more not required, under the engineering vote, but they are not the thirteen that were retired by the late Government. That is what I understand the minister's answer to be, that these are thirteen not required in that service, but they were not retired by the late government. There were others that were retired, but not these thirteen.
No, they were not retired. They have been employed in other branches.

So the method this Government adopts when men are not required in the engineering branch is not the method adopted by the late government of letting them out, but to bring them out of the department into the contingencies vote under civil government.
This year we are carrying some twenty-three vacancies. The late Government carried thirty-three last year.

What I stated is correct, then, so that whereas Providence
Supply-Public Works

and the late government made the reductions the minister himself is wholly responsible for the increases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A very unusual combination.
They often worked together.

I notice that the minister in one of his explanations gave as one of the reasons for the increase, the transfer of thirteen clerks, but what I cannot understand is why these thirteen are brought from one branch of the Department of Public Works into another where there is no work for them to do. If the minister could show that there was work for them to do, I would not be disposed to press my motion. Why are these men needed in the branch to which they have been transferred?

There has been
a decrease in the amount of work in the engineering branch, but in the accounting branch, I am advised, there has been some increase. These people have been transferred to other branches where there has been an increase of work.

How could there be an increase of work in the accounting branch when there is less work going on in the Public Works Department? The Minister of Finance has rather intimated that there was an effort on our part to embarrass the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not say that.
It is fair criticism.

I want to assure the committee and the Finance Minister that no such thought is in my mind, and if the minister could give me a satisfactory explanation I would not press the motion, but I do think we ought to be given some better explanation than has been given so far. If the work of the whole department is decreasing, there must be less work to do in the accounting branch, and if these men are not needed there, they might as well stay where they are. It seems to me we have been given no explanation of that whatever, and until we have, I do not see why this money should be voted.
A large number of these persons have been transferred from the engineering branch to other branches of the service where there are vacancies to be filled.

It is not a case of vacancies because you would not need the extra money for that. You had $15,000 before, and you are getting $31,000 now. You are increasing the number of clerks in this particular branch where there is less work to do. That is what the minister does not explain.

We are not increasing the staff. We are filling vacancies with officials who are not required in other branches of the service. There is no increase. As a matter of fact, there is a decrease in the civil government salaries vote this year.
On account of reductions and resignations that we effected last year.

I am not quite satisfied that this item is right. The minister perhaps is under some disadvantage because he has not yet had sufficient time to familiarize himself with the workings of his department. I think it is only reasonable that he should have more time, but this much has been made clear, and it is some satisfaction to find that it has been made clear, that the whole reduction in this department is due to the action of the late government, that the whole reduction of 145 in the Post Office Department is due to the action of the late government, and that the claim of the Militia Department that 400 were let out on the 1st of April is wholly due to automatic reductions. So that this much applauded action on the part of the Administration in the direction of economy has very little foundation in fact. Only a day or two after these Estimates were brought down I saw some notice in one of the newspapers in the reading room of the number of reductions made in the various departments, but so far as our examination has proceeded, it appears that all these reductions were made under the late government, and so far as any one knows, the present Government has not made any reductions whatever in the Civil Service staff. That much has come out in the discussion, so I think if it has cleared up nothing else, the discussion has been worth while.

Would it be possible for the minister to classify by occupation the thirty officials who are to be paid under this contingencies vote?

The minister may be able to refute that presumption, but I think
he should secure the information that would enable him to do so for the committee. speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Trade and Commerce) :
speechtext: When the general Estimates are up and we have under consideration the question of the extension of trade I shall be very glad to go fully into the subject of trade with Mexico and other ;parts of the world. It is only fair to say that my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) initiated an inquiry into the possibility of trade with Mexico; I found the documents which indicate this on file when I assumed the administration of the department. We are making a careful study of the possibilities of trade with that country and also as to the wisdom of encouraging the development of such trade owing to the recent disturbance in Mexico. It is a little premature just now to make a statement as to whether or not the Government will subsidize a line of steamers to Mexico. I am sure my hon. friend will agree with me that in such a matter it is better to move slowly, and be sure of results, rather than to encourage a trade that might not perhaps prove profitable to the Canadian people. I hope, however, that when the main Estimates come up we will be able to afford information that will not only be satisfactory to my hon. friend but encouraging to the country.

May I ask the minister to explain why such a large increase has been made in the salary of the director of commercial intelligence, viz., from $6,000 to $6,900? That official is now receiving a larger stipend than the deputy minister?
That is one of the very questions I asked myself when going through the estimates-why it was that the director of commercial intelligence was paid a higher salary than the deputy minister.
He never was.

He is.
Mr. MEIGHfiN: Yes, he is now.
I understand this is under the re-arrangement made by the Civil Service Commission and the general statutory allowance made in the regulations provided under the Civil Service Act.
I really do not like to doubt the minister.
The Civil Service Commission fixed this salary, and it was submitted to the previous government and they approved the increase authorized by the commission.
From $6,000 to $6,900.? Who is the Director of Commercial Intelligence.
Mr. Poussette.
And the Civil Service Commission fixed his salary at $6,900- over a deputy minister?
With the possibility of his going to $7,200, and the government of which my hon. friend was the Prime Minister approved of the regulation.

I have no recollection of it. I would like to be favoured with the papers by the minister. I am sure he has looked it up or he would not make the statement, but I do not think there is any other similar instance in all the civil government estimates.
I quite agree with my hon. friend on that.

Will the hon. gentleman explain why there is added to the list a publicity assistant and a junior departmental librarian as well? One would not think it was time to add those officers, and a senior photographer as well. I am told a lantern slide artist has been added also. I would like to hear the minister attempt to load this on the Civil Service Commission.

For the information of my hon. friend, I may say to him that I have such confidence in my predecessors that I have accepted these estimates, number of employees and the salaries, plus the usual allowance made under the Civil Service regulations, exactly as I found them when I came into office, and I shall have to look to my hon. friend for an explanation.

That will not go down at all. It was the habit, under the old gov-

ernment, for the minister to review the estimates submitted to him by the officers of the department. The time for reviewing estimates had not arrived on the 29th December. The time for reviewing the estimates by the officers came between that time and the time when the hon. minister assumed office. That is the unfortunate thing about it. These estimates would have been reviewed had there not been a change. However, the minister considered it his duty to take whatever was put before him. Really it is just as disgraceful to load it in that way on the late government as it would be to load it on the Civil Service Commission. Has the minister no better explanation as to why these offices were added? I know the numbers are the same as the year before, but if the minister had not created these offices there would be a diminution. These were not here before. The minister can see no provision was made last year for them. These were additions. If they had not been created, then there would have been diminution, but not by any act of the minister. I will venture to suggest that he has not retired one man or one woman from the department.
Or added one.

Oh yes. How do you account for asking the House to vote $1,320 for a lantern slide artist, when the House did not vote a dollar last year? Then we have the publicity assistant. These were not in last year's estimates at all. The estimates may have been submitted to the minister by his officers, but what I am complaining of is not the work of the officers but the work of the minister. Why are these additions made?

Surely the hon. gentleman would not expect me immediately on coming into office to go through the department and discharge men that his ministers had placed in office, as between the time the Estimates were passed last year and the time I assumed charge of the department?
The minister last year could not place anyone in office unless there was a salary for him. There was no salary for him last year. These are salaries to be provided next year.
I found that out when I came into office.
How was this lantern slide artist paid? , There was no salary for him last year.
He would be paid out of contingencies would he not? However, during the interim, he has been re-classified and given a standing, and I found this condition when I assumed office.
If the minister has the same amount for contingencies this year as last year, why does he not reduce his contingencies by this amount?
Would the hon. gentleman recommend that we reduce them?
I would, yes. I observe that I do not get any favourable response.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. COPP (Secretary of State) :
speechtext: I venture to say that the reduction is not really fifteen, because it is a transfer from one Classification to another. I think the real reduction is only six.
When was that made?
Made by the deputy minister before I came in or since.

The 'hon. minister
surely would not suggest that the deputy would dismiss people without his knowledge; so that if he knows of no reduction, these were all made before he came in.

These items were given to me by the deputy. I made no reduction myself, but I was glad to see a slight reduction in these estimates, and if there is any credit due to my hon. friend in this respect, I am the last one to attempt to take it away from him.

I am not bothering about that, but I want to know the facts. There is a reduction of six in the number of employees. He says he made no reduction himself. He retired nobody. I do not suppose his staff under him are retiring people without the knowledge of the minister, and consequently all the retirements

were made before he came into office; so that the reduction is entirely due to his predecessor in office. Is that not correct?

The reductions were probably made before the hon. gentleman came into office.

I made no reduction except
what was recommended to me by my officials.

Will the minister tell
me one single retirement that was recommended to him and that he made?

I accepted the statement
given to me by my officials when they brought the estimates to me.

I wonder why the minister is there. We may quite as well have this put before us simply by the deputy. The minister does not answer my question at all. There is an increase
in salaries.

I do not think there are
any except statutory increases.

Is the minister's
enthusiasm for economy such that he feels he could make some reduction in the Public Archives? I do not wish to say a word against the retention of the work of the archives; every country must provide for its archives. Still, if the minister is consumed with a passion for economy, the reproductive activities of the country would not be at all impaired if economy was applied to the Department of Public Archives.

I think the work of the
Archives branch with regard to the affairs

of this Dominion should be extended rather than curtailed. We have in the person of Dr. Doughty, deputy minister of this branch, a man who has done splendid service and who has collected a great mass of data regarding matters relating to the whole Dominion. I have had a number of compliments paid to Dr. Doughty through me on the splendid work that he has performed. I have not yet had an opportunity of studying the department myself; but if there is an opportunity of making any reductions or bringing about economy, I would be very glad to assist and co-operate with all hon. members. I feel it would be a splendid thing and an afternoon, not lost, if every hon. gentleman would make it a point to visit the Archives branch some afternoon in order to see the splendid work carried on by it. I take no credit for the work myself; but I feel that we have in Dr. Doughty a gentleman who is doing splendid work in this branch. I am sure, if I have the privilege of presiding ever this branch for another year, I shall be able to give more information to the committee in regard to it. If there is any reduction my right hon. friend could suggest that could be made without interfering with the work of the branch, I should be glad to consider it.

The third official in the list is the Assistant Director of War Trophies. These war trophies would, I should think, have been distributed months ago amongst the various municipalities and public bodies to which they were destined. In my province, you will see them dotted all over the landscape, and we are very proud to have them. Is this man to be a permanent employee of the department, and are we to keep him forever at a salary of $3,360? There would seem to be an opportunity for the minister to exercise that disposition of which he has just given verbal testimony.
The information I have is that we have a very large number of these war trophies yet on hand for distribution.
I notice in this list a book binder at $31 a week We had one lone book binder last year. This year we seem to have abolished him. Can the minister tell us why?
Economy.

Are we going to do without any binding? How are we going to preserve these valuable documents unless we have a book binder?

Questions
We replaced him by a high binder.

A hide-bound Tory?
Have we abolished book-binding altogether in the public archives?

I cannot give my hon. friend the information. I do not know whether they had a book binder there, or whether his services have been dispensed with or not. The item is a small one, and I fancy the books will be bound whether this official is kept at this wage or not.
Bound by whom?

Would it not be likely that, under the efficiency efforts of the late government in the improvement of the Printing Bureau, in the gathering together of a large number of miscellaneous small printing plants under the bureau and the reduction of the cost of that establishment, this work is performed now at the Printing Bureau instead of at the Archives?
Is that a fact or merely a theory?
I think it is a fact and a testimony to the efficiency of the late government.
And $500,000 a year was saved in the bureau in addition to the fact of our taking care of the extra work.

How is it then that
the hon. gentlemen find themselves on the other side of the House?

Because of the failure of my hon. friend and those around him to state these facts to the electorate, and because, where my hon. friend did not have the hardihood to state himself what was in the interest of his party in the way of misrepresentation, there was always around him and through the press an army which was competent to do that.
Therefore, I conclude the people of Canada were fools.
The hon. gentleman is not very far wrong.
Oh, oh.

I really thought the hon. member had used the word "fooled." The hon. gentleman is only wrong to this
extent, that the "s" should be changed to "ed."
